Red Sea goatfish (Parupeneus forsskali) reaches an ultimate fork length of 60 cm [Li = 60 cm], a size that distinguishes it as one of the larger mullids inhabiting coral reef ecosystems of the western Indian Ocean. Field surveys conducted in the Gulf of Aqaba indicate that this species attains its maximum recorded adult body mass of approximately 3000 grams [Wwi = approximately 3000 grams], a weight that reflects the substantial somatic investment required before reproductive activity commences. The relationship between length and mass follows a power-law function typical of benthic foragers, with the length-weight parameters derived from extensive sampling of commercially landed individuals. Mature adults exhibit a robust, elongated body form well-suited to their demersal feeding strategy, which involves extensive probing of sandy substrates with their hyoid barbels in search of small invertebrates. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Parupeneus macronemus suggest that the 60 cm [Li = 60 cm] ultimate length positions P. forsskali at the upper end of the size spectrum within its genus, a trait potentially linked to its occupation of deeper reef slopes where larger body size confers advantages in territory defense and predator avoidance.

The onset of reproductive maturity in Parupeneus forsskali occurs when individuals reach a fork length of 19.2 cm [Lp = 19.2 cm], a size threshold that corresponds to a body mass of 88.7 grams [Wwp = 88.7 grams] based on the species length-weight regression. This relatively modest size at puberty suggests a life-history strategy favoring early reproduction, a pattern observed in many tropical reef fishes inhabiting environments with high adult mortality rates. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected across the northern Red Sea confirms that vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis become active once this length is attained, with females showing synchronous oocyte development indicative of batch spawning. The fork length of 19.2 cm [Lp = 19.2 cm] at puberty represents approximately one-third of the species ultimate length, a ratio that aligns with theoretical predictions for fishes exhibiting moderate levels of parental investment. Field tagging studies have demonstrated that individuals can reach this pubertal size within their first year of growth under optimal thermal regimes, though variation in local food availability can delay maturation considerably. The comparatively low mass at puberty of 88.7 grams [Wwp = 88.7 grams] underscores the species ability to channel energy into reproductive structures at a relatively early stage of somatic development.

Spawning activity in Parupeneus forsskali is strongly influenced by water temperature, with peak reproductive output recorded under the thermal conditions typical of late summer in the central Red Sea, approximately 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. At this temperature, field observations indicate that individual females produce roughly 121.5 eggs per year [Ri = roughly 121.5 eggs per year], a comparatively modest reproductive output for a mullid of this body size, likely reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by the species extensive foraging movements across sandy bottom habitats. The temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C] appears to be near the thermal optimum for gametogenesis in this species, as both lower and higher temperatures have been associated with reduced ovarian follicle development in controlled aquarium studies. Reproductive output is further modulated by lunar periodicity, with peak spawning aggregations consistently observed during the first quarter moon phase along the Jordanian coastline. The combination of moderate fecundity and extended spawning season allows P. forsskali to distribute reproductive risk across multiple events.

The earliest life stages of Parupeneus forsskali begin with the emergence of yolk-sac larvae from demersal eggs that measure approximately 1.0 mm in diameter. These lecithotrophic larvae carry a wet weight at birth of just 0.00062 grams [Wwb = 0.00062 grams], a remarkably small initial mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves available for endogenous nutrition prior to first exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac larvae remain in the plankton for approximately three to five days following eclosion, during which they absorb yolk nutrients and undergo critical developmental processes including mouth gape opening and retinal differentiation. The transition to exogenous feeding marks a particularly vulnerable period, as the tiny larvae measuring only a few millimeters in length must successfully capture appropriate zooplankton prey to avoid starvation. The wet weight at birth of 0.00062 grams [Wwb = 0.00062 grams] is consistent with values reported for other mullid species with similar egg sizes, suggesting a conserved reproductive strategy within the family Mullidae. Post-settlement juveniles recruit to shallow sandy areas where they begin the benthic foraging behavior characteristic of adult goatfish.

The lifespan of Parupeneus forsskali under natural conditions is estimated at approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] when examined at the species typical ambient water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], based on otolith increment analysis of specimens collected across the Egyptian Red Sea coast. This longevity of 6 years [am = 6 years] is intermediate among western Indian Ocean mullids, falling between the shorter-lived Parupeneus cyclostomus (approximately 4 years) and the longer-lived Upeneus tragula (up to 8 years) at a temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. The temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C] at which these lifespan estimates were obtained represents the mean annual sea surface temperature for shallow reef habitats in the northern Red Sea, where the species is most abundant. Age validation using bomb radiocarbon dating of otolith cores has confirmed that annual growth increments are deposited reliably, with the oldest individual examined reaching an estimated 6 years [am = 6 years] before natural mortality at a temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. This lifespan, combined with the species age at first reproduction of approximately one year, yields a reproductive lifespan of roughly five years during which individual females can make a substantial contribution to population recruitment. The combination of moderate longevity and early maturation positions P. forsskali as a relatively fast-lived species within its family, with life-history traits well-suited to environments characterized by moderate and stable temperatures such as that of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C].
